newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia calls currency speculators unscrupulous.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia calls currency speculators unscrupulous.

text.p: Malaysia renewed its attack on currency speculators on Monday, with Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi dubbing them unscrupulous traders bent on unholy actions.

In an opening address to a meeting of leading Asian and Western nations, Abdullah said it was troubling that ASEAN economies "continue to be bedevilled by currency fluctuations caused by hostile elements bent on such unholy actions".
"It is really the height of international criminality that the fate of millions could be subject to the mercy of a few unscrupulous traders.
"We in ASEAN have resolved to intensify actions to take counter measures. It is time that we recognise these actions for what they really are, namely villainous acts of sabotage," Abdullah said.
He was addressing a meeting of the nine members of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) and their 10 so-called dialogue partners.

ASEAN comprises Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore, Indonesia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Brunei, Burma and Laos. The dialogue partners are the United States, Japan, China, Russia, South Korea, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India and the European Union.

ASEAN held its annual foreign ministers' conference last week, while ministers held political and security discussions with leading Asian and Western powers under the umbrella of the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) on Sunday.
On Monday and Tuesday, ASEAN meets the dialogue partners again to discuss regional and international issues ranging from economic cooperation to the fight against drugs and terrorism.
Cambodia and international efforts led by ASEAN to broker a settlement to the political crisis there have dominated the meetings so far.

But anger among some ASEAN members, primarily Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia, over recent speculative attacks on their currencies are expected to come up in talks on Monday and Tuesday.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad has openly accused American billionaire George Soros of leading the assault. Soros has denied attempts to destabilise Asian currencies.
ASEAN Secretary-General Ajit Singh outlined on Monday the thrust of ASEAN economic cooperation, which aims to introduce a free trade area in the region by 2003.
But Cambodia still cast a shadow over the 30th anniversary ASEAN sessions.
"It is unfortunate that the meeting has been clouded somewhat by the Cambodian issue, but I suppose it was inevitable," Singh told Reuters.

He said three ASEAN foreign ministers headed by Indonesia's Ali Alatas -- dubbed The Three Amigos -- would go to Phnom Penh as soon as Cambodian strongman Hun Sen had clarified his attitude towards mediation to end the political crisis there.
"They will go, but they will wait until we get the clarification from (Foreign Minister) Ung Huot on behalf of Hun Sen," Singh said.

Earlier this month, Second Prime Minister Hun Sen rebuffed an ASEAN mediation effort to end the crisis in Cambodia, precipitated when he staged a bloody putsch to oust coalition colleague and First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
Along with Cambodia, Burma figured prominently in Sunday's debate following its admittance to ASEAN together with Laos last week.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright took a tough approach, acknowledging Burma's membership in ASEAN but telling other member states to exert influence on Rangoon to respect human rights and democracy.
She said the "lack of legitimate government" in Burma threatened the stability of the whole region and also accused the Rangoon authorities of protecting and profiting from the drug trade.
